ask: Why is it on the path?
cards: The oldest surviving work of Mongolian literature tells of Temüjin's youth and his struggles with the Tatars and Merkits before his rise to power.
Proclaimed Genghis Khan at a kurultai in 1206, Temüjin built the largest contiguous land empire in history, which split into rival khanates after 1260.
A grandson of Genghis Khan, Batu led the western campaign of 1236 to 1242 into Rus', Poland and Hungary, then ruled the western steppe from Sarai.
From Sarai on the Volga, Jochi's descendants took tribute from the Rus' princes for over two centuries, until the Great Stand on the Ugra in 1480 ended Moscow's tribute.
Another grandson led the Mongol campaigns into south-western Asia in the 1250s, sacking Baghdad in 1258 and ending the Abbasid Caliphate.
Hulagu's khanate in Persia and Iraq became a Persianised Islamic state under Ghazan, who converted in 1295 and began sweeping reforms with Rashid al-Din.
Genghis Khan allotted Central Asia's steppe and Silk Road cities to his son Chagatai; the khanate turned Muslim and Turkic and lost Transoxiana to Timur by 1370.
Great Khan and founder of the Yuan Dynasty, Kublai completed the conquest of the Song in 1279, and his disputed succession helped break the empire apart.
Ruling China from Dadu, the Yuan linked it to Persia and Europe across the Mongol network until floods, inflation and the Red Turbans brought it down in 1368.
Timur, produced by the Chagatai realm, conquered from Anatolia to the borders of China, and his heirs made Samarkand and Herat centres of painting, poetry and astronomy.
